text: An unauthenticated scan interacts with a target purely over the network, with no credentials at all — exactly the position an outside attacker is in before compromising anything. It sees open ports, the service listening on each one, and whatever version banner that service is willing to advertise. That's genuinely useful: it's exactly what an unauthenticated attacker scanning your network would see too, but it's inherently limited to what's visible from the outside.

An authenticated scan gives the scanner valid credentials — a local administrator account connecting over SMB or WinRM on Windows, or an SSH account on Linux — and has it log in the way an administrator would. From inside, it enumerates every installed application and exact version, checks patch levels against the operating system's own records, and inspects configuration and registry settings directly, finding local vulnerabilities that never touch the network at all.

Take a Windows server: an unauthenticated scan sees only that port 443 is open and reports on the web service there. An authenticated scan of that same server, logging in with a domain account, additionally finds an outdated PDF reader, three missing security updates, and a weakened registry setting — none of which ever appear on the network, and none of which the unauthenticated scan could possibly have seen.

Authenticated scanning is unambiguously more thorough, because the scanner is looking at ground truth instead of inferring from the outside. The real cost isn't performance — it's credential management. Scanning accounts typically need broad administrative access across every system scanned, making them a high-value target if stored carelessly, and someone has to maintain, rotate, and restrict them across potentially thousands of machines.

That's exactly why mature vulnerability management programs run authenticated scans as the primary, scheduled assessment, while still running occasional unauthenticated scans to validate what an attacker with zero access would actually be able to see from outside.
